whyThisMatters: Real fleet decisions are fast — a permit, an invoice, an alert, and you don't always get time to research whether it's genuine. This game trains your reflex for good habits, and helps you catch things that only sound safe.
rememberThis: This month's habit to carry forward: fast instinct is good, but some things only sound safe — a matching PO number, an official-looking notice, a senior title attached to urgency. When you are not sure, slow down and check before you trust the label.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group which bubble tricked them. Most people get at least one of the trick bubbles wrong on their first try.
Ask why a matching PO number on a dry-dock invoice doesn't prove new bank details are genuine.
Ask why a number printed on a port-authority notice might not be trustworthy.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is tapping anything official-looking — a matching PO number, a senior title, a notice with the right logo — without checking it through the company's own known channel. The trick bubbles are there to catch that habit.

bubbles.text: Follow the permit-to-work process
bubbles.why: Permits make sure risky work is approved by the right people, not an impostor.

bubbles.text: Call back to confirm bank changes
bubbles.why: A call to a known number exposes fake bank-change requests before money moves.

bubbles.text: Check tracking alerts in the console
bubbles.why: The real console shows true alerts; a fake link can steal your login.

bubbles.text: Verify port notices with the liaison
bubbles.why: A known contact can confirm a notice is real before you pay or act on it.

bubbles.text: Require a signed charter addendum
bubbles.why: A signed addendum proves a change is genuine and stops fake route orders.

bubbles.text: Report suspicious system alerts
bubbles.why: Reporting lets the IT team investigate before the alert tricks anyone else.

bubbles.text: Check the invoice sender's domain
bubbles.why: Look-alike domains are how fraudsters send fake invoices that look genuine.

bubbles.text: Escalate unverified redirect requests
bubbles.why: Redirect orders are a known scam; a second check stops a vessel being misdirected.

bubbles.text: Confirm vendors via a known contact
bubbles.why: A saved contact reaches the real vendor, not an impostor using a new number.

bubbles.text: Hold payment until bank change checked
bubbles.why: Stopping to verify costs little; a payment to a fraudster is rarely recovered.

bubbles.text: Skip the permit when it's urgent
bubbles.why: Scammers use urgency so you bypass the permit that would expose them.

bubbles.text: Change vendor bank details by email
bubbles.why: Emails are easily faked, so fraudsters use them to redirect payments.

bubbles.text: Click a tracking alert link
bubbles.why: Fake alert links lead to look-alike sites that steal your login.

bubbles.text: Pay a port fee via an email link
bubbles.why: Fake fee emails send your money straight to criminals.

bubbles.text: Redirect a vessel without an addendum
bubbles.why: Without a signed addendum, a fake order could send a ship somewhere it shouldn't go.

bubbles.text: Ignore a mismatched invoice domain
bubbles.why: A domain that doesn't match is a classic sign the invoice is fake.

bubbles.text: Trust an unverified chat request
bubbles.why: Anyone can pose as a colleague in chat; an unchecked request may be fraud.

bubbles.text: Skip the change-approval step
bubbles.why: Approval steps catch fraudulent changes; skipping one lets them through.

bubbles.text: Treat a senior title as proof
bubbles.why: Criminals copy executive titles because people tend to obey them.

bubbles.text: Bypass safety sign-off to save time
bubbles.why: Sign-off protects crew and ship; a faked rush request can cause real harm.

bubbles.text: Use two-person permit sign-off
bubbles.why: Two people checking makes it much harder for one tricked person to approve fraud.

bubbles.text: Check the PO on dry-dock invoices
bubbles.why: A missing or wrong PO number quickly reveals a fake invoice.

bubbles.text: Call the number printed on a notice
bubbles.why: A scam notice's number connects you to the scammer, not the real authority.

bubbles.text: Trust an alert that looks right
bubbles.why: Scam alerts copy real logos and layouts, so looks alone prove nothing.
